# Introduction {#sec-intro}

The `forestsearch` package (León et al., 2024) implements an exploratory
subgroup identification procedure for clinical trials with survival
endpoints, using the Cox proportional-hazards model as the core
estimator. Version 0.2.0 extends this framework to **generalized linear
model (GLM) outcomes**, enabling exploratory subgroup search for binary,
continuous, and count endpoints within the same methodology.

This document provides an overview of the GLM extension: how to access
the development branch, a conceptual summary of the four simulation
studies validating and demonstrating the new capabilities, a discussion
of threshold specification for each outcome type, and a comparison of the
two subgroup identification engines --- ForestSearch (FS) and the
standalone GRF module --- as applied to non-survival data.


# Accessing the GLM Extension {#sec-access}

The GLM extension is developed on the `feature/glm-extension` branch of
the public repository. To install the development version:

```r
# Install from the development branch
remotes::install_github(
  "larry-leon/forestsearch",
  ref = "feature/glm-extension"
)
```

If `remotes` is not installed:

```r
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github(
  "larry-leon/forestsearch",
  ref = "feature/glm-extension"
)
```

To clone the branch for local development and contribute:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/larry-leon/forestsearch.git
cd forestsearch
git checkout feature/glm-extension
```

Or, within an existing clone:

```bash
git fetch origin
git checkout feature/glm-extension
git pull origin feature/glm-extension
```

**Dependencies.** The GLM extension requires the same packages as the
survival version (`survival`, `grf`, `glmnet`, `data.table`,
`doFuture`, `foreach`, `future`) plus `speff2trial` for the ACTG175
simulation vignettes.

::: {.callout-note}
## CRAN release plan

The `feature/glm-extension` branch targets CRAN submission as version
0.2.0. The `master` branch contains the current CRAN release (v0.1.0),
which supports survival outcomes only. The GLM branch is
backward-compatible: all v0.1.0 survival analyses continue to work
without modification.
:::


# Simulation Studies {#sec-sims}

Four simulation documents validate the GLM implementation and
characterize its operating properties. Each builds a data-generating
mechanism (DGM) from an existing clinical trial dataset, calibrates an
interaction effect to achieve a target subgroup effect size, and
evaluates ForestSearch's ability to detect and correctly classify the
subgroup across hundreds to thousands of Monte Carlo replicates.


## Survival Fourway: Proof-of-Concept for the GLM Framework {#sec-fourway}

**Document:** `calibration_survival_fourway.qmd`

### The Poisson–Cox equivalence as a validation anchor

The first simulation does not introduce a new clinical setting: it
validates the GLM machinery itself. The key insight is the
**Poisson–Cox equivalence**: when survival data are analysed by Poisson
regression with a log follow-up time offset, the resulting incidence rate
ratio (IRR) estimates the same quantity as the Cox partial likelihood
hazard ratio, and their variances are asymptotically identical.

Specifically, for the Cox model $\lambda(t; V) = \lambda_0(t)\exp(\beta
V)$ the partial likelihood score gives $\widehat\beta \approx N(\beta,
4/d)$, where $d$ is the number of events. For the Poisson+offset model
$\log E[Y_i] = \beta_0 + \beta V_i + \log(t_i)$, the Fisher information
for $\beta$ is $I(\beta) = d_0 + d_1 = D$ (total events), so
$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta) \approx 4/D$. Because $D = d$, the
two effective information quantities are identical:

$$
d_{\text{eff}}^{\text{Poisson}} = D = d^{\text{Cox}}
$$

This equivalence means that the ForestSearch asymptotic approximation
for the per-subgroup detection probability,

$$
p(c_1, c_2;\, d,\, \theta^\dagger(H))
= P\!\left(W_1 + W_2 \ge 2\log c_1,\ \min(W_1,W_2) \ge \log c_2\right),
\quad W_1, W_2 \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(\beta,\, 8/d),
$$

applies unchanged to Poisson+offset data when $d_{\text{eff}} = D$ is
substituted. The GLM approximation formula (`compute_detection_probability_glm()`)
therefore produces **identical numerical output** to the survival formula
(`compute_detection_probability()`) when applied to the same survival
data through either model.

### Study design

The simulation uses the GBSG-based DGM from León et al. (2024): a
super-population of breast cancer patients with a true harm subgroup $H$
defined by ER-low status and pre-menopausal age. Key parameters:

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Sample size $N$ | 700 |
| Subgroup prevalence $p(H)$ | 13% |
| Target HR($H$) | 2.0 |
| Censoring proportion | 46% |
| Analysis time | 84 months |
| Confounders | 7 (z1–z5, size, grade3) |
| H1 / H0 simulations | 2,000 / 5,000 |

The same GBSG null DGM is run twice: once via the established Cox PH
pipeline **(C)** and once via the new GLM pipeline with
`outcome_type = "binary"`, `effect_measure = "IRR"`, and
`offset.name = "y_sim"` (follow-up time) **(A)**. A critical
implementation detail is that the Poisson model's outcome variable is the
**binary event indicator** `event_sim` (0/1), not the observed survival
time `y_sim`; the follow-up time enters as the log-offset, not as the
response.

### Four-way structure

The comparison has four cells: two analytical methods (Cox, Poisson+offset)
crossed with two evaluation modes (asymptotic approximation, Monte Carlo
simulation).

| Label | Method | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **(A)** | Poisson+offset simulation | GLM pipeline |
| **(B)** | GLM approximation ($d_{\text{eff}} = D$) | GLM theory |
| **(C)** | Cox PH simulation | Established pipeline |
| **(D)** | Cox approximation (`compute_detection_probability()`) | Package (Section 2.1) |

The expected outcomes are: **(B)** = **(D)** exactly (both use $d_{\text{eff}} = d$);
**(A)** $\approx$ **(C)** within simulation error; and approximations (B, D)
close to the corresponding simulations (A, C).

Agreement across all four cells simultaneously validates (i) the GLM
variance formula, (ii) the correctness of the Poisson+offset
implementation, and (iii) the GLM simulation infrastructure
(`generate_glm_dgm()`, `simulate_from_glm_dgm()`,
`run_simulation_analysis()`).


## Binary Outcomes: ACTG175 Benefit Subgroup Search {#sec-binary}

**Document:** `actg175_binary_benefit_simulations.qmd`

### Clinical context and benefit-search convention

The ACTG175 trial compared four antiretroviral regimens in HIV-positive
patients (Hammer et al., 1996). Following León et al. (2024, Section
4.2), the simulation focuses on arms 1 (ZDV+ddI combination) versus 3
(ddI monotherapy) and searches for a **benefit subgroup** $Q$: a patient
subset where ddI monotherapy is superior to the combination, identified
by the treatment-switching convention.

ForestSearch's harm-detection machinery is repurposed for benefit
detection by **reversing the treatment labels**: ddI monotherapy is
re-coded as `treat = 1` and ZDV+ddI as `treat = 0`. Under this
re-coding, the benefit subgroup $Q$ appears as a "harm" subgroup in the
search, and the package's `subgroup_notation = "benefit"` flag handles
the back-inversion for reporting. The subgroup-defining variables are:

- $z_1 = 1$: Age $>$ 34 years (median split)
- $z_2 = 1$: Prior antiretroviral exposure $\leq$ 744.5 days (third quartile split)

The binary outcome is CD4 count response at 20 weeks ($\mathtt{cd420} >
\mathtt{cd40}$), a well-established surrogate endpoint.

### DGM and calibration

A logistic regression is fitted to the observed ACTG175 data (arms 1 and
3 only, switched treatment coding) to construct a 5,000-subject
super-population. The interaction parameter `k_inter` shifts the
log-odds of a positive CD4 response for Q members under ddI
(treat = 1). Calibration searches for the `k_inter` value that achieves
OR$(Q) = 2.0$ on the switched scale — corresponding to
OR$(Q) = 0.50$ on the original treatment scale, i.e. a strong benefit
for Q patients receiving ddI monotherapy.

### Study design

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Sample size $N$ | 1,000 |
| Subgroup definition | $z_1 = 1 \cap z_2 = 1$ (Age $>$ 34 AND Preanti $\leq$ 745 days) |
| Subgroup prevalence $p(Q)$ | ~25% |
| Target OR$(Q)$ — switched scale | 2.0 |
| Target OR$(Q)$ — original scale | 0.50 |
| Confounders | 12 ($z_1$–$z_{12}$, binary) |
| H1 / H0 simulations | 2,500 / 25,000 |
| Methods compared | ForestSearch (FS) + standalone GRF |

Both ForestSearch and the standalone GRF module (`grf.subg.harm.glm()`)
are run on every replicate, enabling a direct operating-characteristic
comparison.


## Continuous Outcomes: CD4 Change in ACTG175 {#sec-continuous}

**Document:** `actg175_continuous_simulations.qmd`

### Endpoint and model

Rather than binarising the CD4 response, this simulation uses the raw
CD4 count change from baseline to 20 weeks ($\mathtt{cd420} -
\mathtt{cd40}$) as a continuous endpoint. The effect measure is the
**mean difference (MD)** between treatment arms within the subgroup,
estimated via a Gaussian GLM with identity link:

$$
E[\text{CD4 change}_i] = \mu_0 + \beta \cdot \text{treat}_i,
\quad \text{treat} \in \{0, 1\}
$$

Subgroup identification proceeds on the MD scale: a candidate subgroup
must satisfy $\widehat{\text{MD}} \geq c_1$ in the full subgroup and
$\widehat{\text{MD}} \geq c_2$ in each random split.

### DGM and calibration

The DGM follows the same ACTG175 structure as the binary simulation:
switched treatment labels, same confounder set ($z_1$–$z_{12}$), same
subgroup definition ($z_1 = 1 \cap z_2 = 1$). Under the Gaussian model,
the interaction parameter `k_inter` maps **linearly** to MD$(Q)$:
$\text{MD}(Q) = \beta_T + k_{\text{inter}}$, where $\beta_T$ is the
fitted main treatment coefficient. This makes calibration considerably
simpler than the binary (logistic) case. The target is MD$(Q) = +40$
cells/$\mu$L on the switched scale.

The DGM preserves the residual standard deviation $\hat\sigma$ from the
baseline Gaussian GLM fit, ensuring realistic noise levels in simulated
datasets.

### Study design

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Sample size $N$ | 1,000 |
| Outcome | CD4 change (cells/$\mu$L) |
| Target MD$(Q)$ — switched scale | +40 cells/$\mu$L |
| H1 / H0 simulations | 2,500 / 5,000 |
| Methods compared | ForestSearch (FS) only |

The standalone GRF module is not run for continuous outcomes in this
document. Variable screening within ForestSearch uses Gaussian LASSO
(`glmnet` with `family = "gaussian"`) instead of the binomial or Cox
variants used in the other pipelines.


## Survival Benefit Search: ACTG175 with Cox PH {#sec-survival-benefit}

**Document:** `actg175_survival_benefit_simulations.qmd`

This fourth simulation applies the **established Cox PH** pipeline to
the ACTG175 trial for benefit subgroup detection in time-to-event data,
serving as a survival-domain analog to the binary benefit simulation. The
outcome is time to AIDS-defining event or death (converted from days to
months). The same treatment-switching convention is applied, with
thresholds on the hazard ratio scale. ForestSearch and the GRF standalone
module are both evaluated. This document demonstrates that the
benefit-search framework extends naturally to the ACTG175 survival
endpoint and provides a direct basis for comparing survival and binary
operating characteristics under the same trial and subgroup definition.


# Effect and Consistency Thresholds {#sec-thresholds}

ForestSearch gates subgroup selection at two sequential checkpoints. A
candidate subgroup $H$ is retained only if both are satisfied in a given
bootstrap replicate:

1. **Screening threshold $c_1$**: the estimated effect in $H$ must
   exceed $c_1$ (on the effect measure's natural scale).
2. **Consistency threshold $c_2$**: the effect must exceed $c_2$ in each
   random half-split of $H$.

The proportion of replicates in which **both** conditions hold must
reach `pconsistency.threshold` (default 0.90) for the subgroup to be
reported. Together, $c_1$, $c_2$, and `pconsistency.threshold` determine
the procedure's false-positive rate (FPR) and power.

## Threshold specification by outcome type

For survival outcomes, León et al. (2024, Section 3) established
$(c_1, c_2) = (1.25, 1.0)$ on the HR scale as defaults providing
an approximate 12% FPR at $N = 700$. For GLM outcomes these defaults
require reconsideration because the effective information $d_{\text{eff}}$
depends on the outcome distribution, as shown in the following table:

| Outcome | Link | $\kappa$ | $d_{\text{eff}}$ |
|---------|------|---------|-----------------|
| Cox PH | log-HR | $(1 - p_c)$ | $d$ (events) |
| Poisson + offset | log-IRR | $\bar\mu$ | $D$ (events) |
| Binomial | logit | $\bar p(1-\bar p)$ | $n_H \bar p(1-\bar p)$ |
| Gaussian | identity | $1/\sigma^2$ | $n_H / \sigma^2$ |

For binary outcomes with a typical event rate of 30–50%, $d_{\text{eff}}
= n_H \bar p(1-\bar p) < n_H/4$, which is generally smaller than the
number of events $d$ for survival data with similar subgroup sizes. This
means the Cox defaults $(1.25, 1.0)$ are **less conservative** for binary
outcomes and would yield FPR substantially above 12% unless thresholds
are raised.

## Survival Fourway

The Cox defaults $(c_1, c_2) = (1.25, 1.0)$ apply directly to the
Poisson+offset analysis as well, since $d_{\text{eff}}^{\text{Poisson}} =
D = d^{\text{Cox}}$. This is precisely the point of the four-way
comparison: verifying that no threshold adjustment is needed when
switching from Cox PH to Poisson+offset on the same survival data.

## Binary outcomes (OR scale)

The binary simulations use an elevated threshold pair on the OR scale:

$$
c_1 = 1/0.60 \approx 1.667, \qquad c_2 = 1/0.80 = 1.25
$$

These are the benefit-search thresholds from León et al. (2024), which
correspond to requiring OR$(Q) \geq 1.667$ under switched treatment
roles (equivalent to OR$(Q) \leq 0.60$ on the original treatment scale).
The elevation relative to the Cox defaults reflects two factors: (i) the
benefit-search convention, where thresholds on the switched scale must be
larger to protect against false detection of the original "harm" null;
and (ii) the reduced $d_{\text{eff}}$ for binary outcomes, which implies
higher per-subgroup type I error at the Cox defaults. An FPR calibration
study (`calibration_binary_leff.qmd`, not included here) characterizes
the FPR under these thresholds as a function of $N$ for the ACTG175
binary DGM.

## Continuous outcomes (MD scale)

For continuous outcomes with `effect_measure = "MD"`, thresholds are on
the **natural difference scale** in the same units as the outcome. The
simulation specifies:

$$
c_1 = 30 \;\text{cells}/\mu\text{L}, \qquad c_2 = 10 \;\text{cells}/\mu\text{L}
$$

These values were chosen given the calibrated subgroup effect MD$(Q) =
+40$ cells/$\mu$L: a candidate must show at least a 30-cell/$\mu$L mean
difference in the full subgroup and at least 10 cells/$\mu$L in each
half-split. Unlike the ratio-scale (HR, OR, IRR) thresholds, there is no
natural "null" value of 1.0; instead, the threshold must be specified
relative to the expected effect size and the noise level $\sigma$ in the
data. Formal FPR calibration for continuous outcomes analogous to the
$L_{\text{eff}}$ framework developed for survival data is a subject of
ongoing work.

## A shared invariance

Across all outcome types, the bootstrap consistency filter
(`pconsistency.threshold = 0.90`) and the minimum subgroup-size
constraints (`n.min`, `d0.min`, `d1.min`) remain unchanged. The
`d0.min` and `d1.min` parameters, which require a minimum number of
events in the control and treatment arms of a candidate subgroup, are
survival-specific (event counts). For binary and continuous outcomes in
the current implementation they are set but play a minor role because
all subjects have observed outcomes; future GLM-native calibration
documents will revisit their specification for non-survival data.


# ForestSearch vs. GRF for GLM Outcomes {#sec-fs-vs-grf}

The package provides two complementary subgroup identification strategies.
Both have been extended to GLM outcomes in v0.2.0, but they differ
substantially in their design philosophies, operating characteristics,
and the role played by thresholds.

## ForestSearch (FS)

ForestSearch proceeds in three stages:

1. **Candidate generation**: LASSO regression (with the appropriate GLM
   family) and, optionally, variable importance screening via GRF
   identify which confounders are most promising as subgroup-defining
   variables. The two-stage option applies LASSO first, then runs GRF
   restricted to the LASSO-selected variables.

2. **Enumeration**: all subgroup definitions consistent with the selected
   variables and the `maxk` depth limit are evaluated. For each
   candidate, the effect estimate is compared against $c_1$.

3. **Consistency filter**: the dataset is randomly split, and the effect
   in each half must exceed $c_2$. This is repeated across `fs.splits`
   random splits; the candidate is retained only if the consistency
   criterion is met in at least `pconsistency.threshold` $\times 100$\%
   of splits.

For GLM outcomes, the LASSO step switches family automatically:
`family = "binomial"` (OR, RD), `family = "poisson"` (IRR, IRD),
or `family = "gaussian"` (MD). The consistency filter and enumeration
logic are unchanged. Thresholds $c_1$ and $c_2$ must be calibrated to
the outcome scale as described in @sec-thresholds.

**Strengths.** The bootstrap consistency filter provides strong FPR
control: a subgroup must survive repeated random half-split tests,
which substantially reduces the probability that a spurious signal
passes. The enumeration strategy is exhaustive within the candidate
set, so the identified subgroup is the globally best-scoring definition
(subject to the consistency requirement), not a locally optimal one.

**Limitations.** The threshold dependence is both a strength and a
limitation: thresholds must be calibrated per-DGM and per-outcome-type
to achieve a target FPR. The enumeration step is computationally
intensive for large candidate sets or deep `maxk` values.

## Standalone GRF (`grf.subg.harm.glm()`)

The GRF module is model-free by design. It uses `causal_forest()` from
the `grf` package to estimate conditional average treatment effects
(CATEs) at the individual level, then applies policy trees to partition
the covariate space into treatment-preferring and control-preferring
regions. The subgroup is the region where CATE is most extreme
(most negative CATE under the harm convention, or most positive under
the benefit convention, depending on `adverse_outcome`).

For GLM outcomes, CATEs are estimated on the **risk-difference** (RD)
scale regardless of `effect_measure`, because `causal_forest()` is a
non-parametric estimator of $E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X]$. The only
GLM-specific tuning parameter is `dmin.grf`: the minimum absolute
CATE (in RD units) required for a policy-tree node to qualify as a
subgroup.

**Strengths.** GRF is threshold-free in the sense that it does not
require specifying $c_1$ or $c_2$; only `dmin.grf` needs calibration.
CATEs capture heterogeneity at the individual level before
discretisation, which can make the approach more sensitive when the
true subgroup boundary is smooth rather than defined by a single
covariate cut. The cross-fitted CATE estimates are doubly robust in
large samples.

**Limitations.** Because GRF lacks the bootstrap consistency filter,
its FPR tends to be higher than ForestSearch's at comparable power levels.
For binary outcomes in the ACTG175 simulation, calibration across the
`dmin.grf` grid shows that FPR control requires accepting some power
reduction: at `dmin.grf = 0.02` (2% risk difference), FPR is approximately
9%, compared to ForestSearch's lower FPR at similar detection rates.
GRF also requires larger sample sizes for reliable CATE estimation;
the consistency of the policy-tree partition can be sensitive to
the chosen `min.node.size` and `mtry` hyperparameters.

## Direct comparison in the binary simulation

The binary ACTG175 simulation (`actg175_binary_benefit_simulations.qmd`)
runs both methods on every replicate, enabling a direct comparison. Key
distinctions observed:

- **Detection rate**: GRF achieves comparable or higher detection than
  ForestSearch under $H_1$, particularly at moderate effect sizes, because
  it does not require the effect to survive the consistency filter.

- **FPR control**: ForestSearch provides stronger FPR control under $H_0$.
  The bootstrap consistency filter is the primary mechanism: requiring the
  signal to replicate across 90% of random data splits effectively guards
  against chance associations. GRF's `dmin.grf` threshold controls FPR
  only indirectly, by raising the minimum detectable CATE.

- **Classification concordance**: when both methods detect a subgroup in
  the same replicate, per-subject classification agreement (quantified
  by Cohen's $\kappa$ via `agree.FS.GRF` and `kappa.FS.GRF`) reflects
  the degree to which the two approaches carve the covariate space
  similarly. High concordance confirms they are targeting the same
  underlying subgroup; low concordance suggests the methods are sensitive
  to different aspects of the heterogeneity.

- **Complementarity**: the two methods are designed to be used together.
  ForestSearch provides a formally calibrated result with strong FPR
  control; GRF provides a model-free corroborating screen. Agreement
  between them strengthens the case for a genuine subgroup; disagreement
  prompts further investigation.

For the continuous ACTG175 simulation, only ForestSearch is currently
run. Standalone GRF for continuous outcomes (`grf.subg.harm.glm()` with
a Gaussian response) is implemented in the package but its
calibration is deferred to a future document.

## Summary

| Feature | ForestSearch | Standalone GRF |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| Core estimator | GLM (logistic/Poisson/Gaussian) | Causal forest (non-parametric) |
| Effect scale for screening | Match `effect_measure` (HR, OR, IRR, MD) | Risk difference (always) |
| Threshold parameters | $c_1$, $c_2$, `pconsistency.threshold` | `dmin.grf` |
| FPR mechanism | Bootstrap consistency filter | Minimum CATE threshold |
| FPR control | Stronger | Moderate (requires calibration) |
| Power | Moderate to high | Comparable to higher |
| Subgroup boundary | Exhaustive enumeration | Policy-tree partition |
| Hyperparameter sensitivity | Low (thresholds are interpretable) | Moderate (`min.node.size`, `mtry`) |
| GLM families supported | Binomial, Poisson, Gaussian | All (CATE on RD scale) |
| Benefit search | Via treatment switching + inversion | Via `adverse_outcome` flag |

## A.2 Operating Characteristics Under H1 (Power) {#sec-app-h1}

### Survival Fourway — Cox PH (C) vs. Poisson+offset (A)

GBSG DGM, $N = 700$, 2,000 replicates, true HR$(H) = 2.00$,
HR$(H^c) = 0.66$.

| Metric | (C) Cox PH | (A) Poisson+offset |
|--------|-----------|-------------------|
| Detection rate | 0.833 | 0.880 |
| Sensitivity | 0.718 | 0.701 |
| Specificity | 0.964 | 0.963 |
| PPV | 0.736 | 0.729 |
| NPV | 0.983 | 0.974 |
| Mean $\hat\theta(H)$ | 2.311 (HR) | 2.163 (IRR) |
| Mean $\hat\theta(H^c)$ | 0.639 | 0.654 |
| Mean $\hat\theta$ (ITT) | 0.745 | 0.755 |

Detection, classification, and effect estimates are closely matched
across the two estimators, confirming the GLM pipeline equivalence.


### Binary Benefit — FS vs. GRF

ACTG175 GLM DGM, $N = 1{,}000$, 2,500 replicates, OR$(Q) = 2.01$
(switched scale), OR$(Q^c) = 0.67$.

| Metric | FS | GRF (`dmin` = 0.10) |
|--------|-----|---------------------|
| Detection rate | 0.74 | 0.72 |
| Sensitivity | 0.42 | 0.65 |
| Specificity | 0.88 | 0.79 |
| PPV | 0.59 | 0.54 |
| NPV | 0.87 | 0.96 |
| Estimable replicates | 1,849 / 2,500 (74%) | 1,791 / 2,500 (72%) |
| Avg $|\hat Q|$ | 218 | 417 |
| Mean $\hat\theta(\hat Q)$ | 0.36 (SD 0.11) | 0.51 (SD 0.09) |
| Estimation bias $b^\dagger$ | −28.6% | +1.8% |

FS achieves stronger specificity and PPV while GRF shows better
sensitivity and substantially lower estimation bias (conditional
on selection). GRF's $\hat Q$ is nearly twice as large on average,
partly explaining its higher sensitivity but lower PPV.


### Continuous Benefit — FS only

ACTG175 Gaussian DGM, $N = 1{,}000$, 2,500 replicates, MD$(Q) = 39.7$
cells/$\mu$L (switched scale), MD$(Q^c) = -26.3$.

| Metric | FS |
|--------|----|
| Detection rate | 0.94 |
| Sensitivity | 0.47 |
| Specificity | 0.93 |
| PPV | 0.71 |
| NPV | 0.81 |
| Estimable replicates | 2,359 / 2,500 (94%) |
| Avg $|\hat Q|$ | 205 |
| Mean $\hat\theta(\hat Q)$ | −56.2 (SD 18.8) |
| Estimation bias $b^\dagger$ | +41.3% |

Detection is the highest across all GLM simulations (94%), reflecting
the large absolute effect size (MD = +40) relative to the threshold
($c_1 = 30$). Estimation bias is notable (selected subgroup effects
overestimated by ~41%), consistent with the selection bias inherent in
ForestSearch and analogous to what is observed in the survival setting.


### Survival Benefit — FS vs. GRF

ACTG175 AFT DGM, $N = 1{,}000$, 2,500 replicates, HR$(Q) = 0.49$
(original scale, i.e. switched HR = 2.04), HR$(Q^c) = 0.90$.

| Metric | FS | GRF (`dmin` = 2 months) |
|--------|----|--------------------------|
| Detection rate | 0.88 | 0.98 |
| Sensitivity | 0.46 | 0.49 |
| Specificity | 0.81 | 0.76 |
| PPV | 0.54 | 0.50 |
| NPV | 0.80 | 0.76 |
| Estimable replicates | 2,208 / 2,500 (88%) | 2,455 / 2,500 (98%) |
| Avg $|\hat Q|$ | 290 | 331 |
| Mean $\hat\theta(\hat Q)$ (HR) | 0.40 (SD 0.08) | 0.47 (SD 0.12) |


## A.3 Operating Characteristics Under H0 (FPR) {#sec-app-h0}

| Study | Method | H0 sims | FPR | Note |
|-------|--------|---------|-----|------|
| Survival Fourway | (C) Cox PH | 5,000 | 5.5% | GBSG null, uniform HR = 0.72 |
| Survival Fourway | (A) Poisson+offset | 5,000 | 14.6% | Same data, elevated vs. Cox |
| Binary Benefit | FS | 25,000 | 4.3% | ACTG175 null, OR(ITT) = 0.67 switched |
| Binary Benefit | GRF | 25,000 | 29.5% | `dmin` = 0.10; see note |
| Continuous Benefit | FS | 5,000 | 12.0% | ACTG175 null, MD(ITT) = −26.3 switched |
| Survival Benefit | FS | 20,000 | 49.0% | ACTG175 null, HR(ITT) = 0.82 orig. |
| Survival Benefit | GRF | 20,000 | 89.0% | `dmin` = 2 months; see note |

**Notes.**

- The Poisson+offset FPR (14.6%) is substantially higher than the Cox
  FPR (5.5%) on the same survival data. The two procedures share
  identical identification logic, but the ForestSearch algorithm
  uses Cox PH internally for subgroup evaluation at every node; the
  "Poisson" label refers only to the final estimation step. The
  inflated FPR suggests the current implementation routes subgroup
  *screening* through Cox regardless of `effect_measure`, and the
  discrepancy reflects this mismatch — the Poisson branch evaluates
  effects with a different model than the one used to set thresholds
  under the Cox defaults.

- GRF FPR for binary outcomes (29.5% at `dmin` = 0.10) is high
  relative to FS. The calibration document
  (`grf_dmin_calibration_binary.qmd`) characterised the FPR–power
  tradeoff: `dmin` = 0.02 achieves FPR ≤ 9% while preserving
  ≥ 76% detection. The `dmin` = 0.10 setting used in the production
  run reflects a more conservative power choice (detection ~72%,
  FPR ~30%) and should be re-evaluated for deployment.

- The survival benefit FPR (49% FS, 89% GRF) is inflated because the
  null DGM preserves the ACTG175 trial's real ITT treatment effect
  (HR = 0.84 original, i.e. HR = 1.19 on the switched scale). This
  is close to the threshold $c_1 = 1.667$ for some subgroups when
  combined with the 12-confounder search space and $N = 1{,}000$.
  The benefit-search FPR under a truly null ITT effect would be
  substantially lower. Threshold recalibration for this DGM is
  ongoing.

- The $L_{\text{eff}}$ null calibration from the Survival Fourway at
  $c_1 = 1.25$, $c_2 = 1.0$ yielded simulated FPRs of 5.4%, 6.6%,
  and 5.5% at $N = 300$, 500, and 700 respectively — consistent with
  the paper's target and validating the calibration framework for
  survival data.


## A.4 Approximation Validation (Survival Fourway) {#sec-app-approx}

The four-way table at $n_H = 60$ ($d = 32$ events), $c_1 = 1.25$,
$c_2 = 1.0$:

| | Method | P($\theta = 1.0$) | P($\theta = 0.75$) | P($\theta = 2.0$) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **(D)** Cox Approximation | Approx | 0.194 | 0.050 | 0.825 |
| **(C)** Cox Simulation | Simulation | 0.055 | — | 0.833 |
| **(B)** GLM Approximation | Approx | 0.194 | 0.051 | 0.822 |
| **(A)** GLM Simulation | Simulation | 0.146 | — | 0.880 |

**(B) = (D)** to three decimal places, confirming the
$d_{\text{eff}}^{\text{Poisson}} = D = d^{\text{Cox}}$ equivalence.
Approximation and simulation agree closely under H1:
**(C)** = 0.833 vs **(D)** = 0.825; **(A)** = 0.880 vs **(B)** = 0.822.
The H0 discrepancy between simulated FPRs (C: 5.5%, A: 14.6%) versus
the per-subgroup approximation (B = D: 19.4%) reflects the
$L_{\text{eff}} < 1$ structure for survival data: after calibration,
the corrected approximation aligns with simulation.


## A.5 FS vs. GRF Concordance — Binary Benefit {#sec-app-concordance}

Per-subject classification concordance between FS and GRF across
2,500 H1 replicates (ACTG175 binary, $N = 1{,}000$):

| Concordance metric | Value |
|--------------------|-------|
| Mean agreement (all replicates) | 80.3% (SD 17.0%) |
| Mean Cohen's $\kappa$ | 0.486 (SD 0.406) |
| Median $\kappa$ | 0.416 |
| Both detected $Q$ | 1,570 (63%) |
| FS only | 279 (11%) |
| GRF only | 221 (9%) |
| Neither detected | 430 (17%) |
| Mean agreement \| both detect | 77.0% |
| Mean $\kappa$ \| both detect | 0.500 |

When both methods detect a subgroup in the same replicate ($n = 1{,}570$,
63%), per-subject agreement averages 77% ($\kappa = 0.50$) — moderate
concordance. This reflects the fundamental difference in how each
method partitions the covariate space: FS enumerates binary-factor
intersections exhaustively; GRF partitions via policy trees on the
estimated CATE surface. Disagreement in individual-level assignment
can coexist with agreement on which variables are most informative.


## A.6 Computational Timing {#sec-app-timing}

| Study | H1 sims | H0 sims | Workers | H1 time | H0 time | Total |
|-------|---------|---------|---------|---------|---------|-------|
| Survival Fourway | 2,000 | 5,000 | 121 | 3.2 min | 6.8 min (Cox) / 7.3 min (IRR) | ~20 min |
| Binary Benefit | 2,500 | 25,000 | 12 | 17 min | 130 min | 147.5 min |
| Continuous Benefit | 2,500 | 5,000 | 12 | 11.4 min | 39.3 min | ~51 min |
| Survival Benefit | 2,500 | 20,000 | 115 | 5 min | 39.5 min | ~45 min |

Per-replicate costs on the machines used:

| Study | sec/sim (H1) | sec/sim (H0) |
|-------|-------------|-------------|
| Binary Benefit (12 workers) | 0.4 | 0.3 |
| Continuous (12 workers) | ~0.3 | ~0.5 |
| Survival Benefit (115 workers) | ~0.1 | ~0.1 |

The Binary Benefit study has the highest wall time due to the large H0
budget ($25{,}000$ sims for stable FPR estimation) and modest worker
count (12 physical cores). The Survival Fourway benefits from 121
workers but involves the heavier Cox bootstrap consistency evaluation.
